reference.source: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery / Sabiston Textbook of Surgery
clinicalPearls: Hepatic haemangioma is the commonest benign liver tumour and is usually an incidental finding on imaging in an asymptomatic patient
Most are small and require no treatment; large (giant) lesions may cause dull right upper quadrant discomfort, early satiety, or a mass effect
Contrast imaging shows a characteristic pattern of peripheral nodular enhancement with progressive centripetal fill-in on CT or MRI, which is typically diagnostic
MRI demonstrates a markedly hyperintense lesion on heavily T2-weighted sequences, helping to confirm the diagnosis non-invasively
Percutaneous biopsy is generally avoided because of the theoretical risk of bleeding and because imaging is usually diagnostic
Management is overwhelmingly conservative with reassurance and, for uncertain or enlarging lesions, surveillance; intervention is reserved for significant symptoms, diagnostic doubt, or complications
Kasabach-Merritt syndrome, a consumptive coagulopathy, is a rare association with very large lesions, chiefly in infants
reference.pathophysiology: A hepatic haemangioma is a benign vascular malformation composed of multiple dilated, blood-filled vascular channels lined by a single layer of endothelium and separated by thin fibrous septa. It is thought to be congenital in origin, enlarging by ectasia rather than by cellular proliferation, and its growth can be influenced by hormonal factors such as pregnancy and oestrogen exposure. Blood flow through the lesion is slow, which underlies the characteristic delayed centripetal enhancement on imaging. Very large lesions can trap and consume platelets and clotting factors, producing the Kasabach-Merritt consumptive coagulopathy, and rarely a superficial lesion may bleed after trauma.
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced CT showing peripheral nodular discontinuous enhancement with centripetal fill-in
MRI with heavily T2-weighted sequences for a characteristically bright lesion
Ultrasound (often a well-defined hyperechoic lesion) as an initial or incidental finding
Labelled red-cell scintigraphy in selected diagnostically uncertain cases
Coagulation screen and platelet count if a very large lesion raises concern for consumptive coagulopathy
Interval imaging surveillance for indeterminate or enlarging lesions
redFlags: Spontaneous or traumatic rupture with intraperitoneal haemorrhage and haemodynamic instability (rare but life-threatening)
Consumptive coagulopathy (Kasabach-Merritt syndrome) with a very large lesion
Rapid enlargement or atypical imaging raising doubt about the benign diagnosis
Severe, progressive symptoms from a giant lesion causing mass effect
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent; most haemangiomas remain stable, cause no symptoms, and never require treatment, with an extremely low risk of complications. Even large lesions usually behave benignly, and surgical resection of genuinely symptomatic or complicated lesions gives good long-term results.
pitfalls: Performing percutaneous biopsy of a suspected haemangioma and risking haemorrhage
Misinterpreting the lesion as a metastasis or hepatocellular carcinoma and subjecting the patient to unnecessary intervention
Over-treating small asymptomatic lesions that only need reassurance
Attributing unrelated abdominal symptoms to a small incidental haemangioma
Overlooking coagulopathy in a patient with a very large lesion
references: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
management: Reassure and give no treatment for typical small asymptomatic lesions, the usual approach
Arrange interval imaging surveillance for indeterminate or enlarging lesions
Reserve surgical resection or enucleation for genuinely symptomatic giant lesions, diagnostic uncertainty or complications
Counsel on oestrogen avoidance and around pregnancy, given the hormonal influence on growth
Avoid percutaneous biopsy because of bleeding risk and because imaging is usually diagnostic
Monitor coagulation and platelets in very large lesions for Kasabach-Merritt consumptive coagulopathy
Refer to hepatobiliary surgery for large, symptomatic or complicated tumours, with transarterial embolisation as an alternative in selected cases
